content: Urinary incontinence is a prevalent and potentially disabling condition that significantly impacts the quality of life of affected women and imposes substantial health and economic burdens on society. Stress urinary incontinence, the most common subtype, is characterized by the involuntary leakage of urine during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure, such as coughing, sneezing, or physical exertion. Open retropubic colposuspension is a surgical intervention designed to address this condition by elevating the tissues surrounding the bladder neck and proximal urethra, thereby improving urethral closure and reducing incontinence. The primary objective of the review was to evaluate the effectiveness of open retropubic colposuspension in treating urinary incontinence in women. A secondary aim was to assess the safety of the procedure, particularly in terms of adverse events associated with the surgery. The review included 55 randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving a total of 5,417 women diagnosed with stress or mixed urinary incontinence. The studies were assessed for methodological quality, risk of bias, and relevance, and data were extracted and analyzed by the authors. The overall cure rates for open retropubic colposuspension ranged from 68.9% to 88.0%. Evidence from two small studies indicated that open retropubic colposuspension resulted in lower incontinence rates compared to conservative treatments. Similarly, one trial demonstrated that this surgical approach was more effective than anticholinergic therapy. When compared to anterior colporrhaphy, six trials showed that open retropubic colposuspension was associated with significantly lower incontinence rates, with this benefit persisting over time. Specifically, the risk ratio (RR) for incontinence was 0.46 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.72) within the first year, 0.37 (95% CI 0.27 to 0.51) at one to five years, and 0.49 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.75) beyond five years. In comparison with suburethral sling procedures, including traditional slings, transvaginal tape (TVT), and transobturator tape, no significant differences in incontinence rates were observed across all evaluated time periods. Subjective assessments yielded RRs of 0.90 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.18) within one year, 1.18 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.39) between one and five years, and 1.11 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.27) beyond five years. Objective assessments showed RRs of 1.24 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.67) within one year, 1.12 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.54) between one and five years, and 0.70 (95% CI 0.30 to 1.64) beyond five years. However, subgroup analyses revealed that traditional slings were more effective than open colposuspension in the medium and long term, with RRs of 1.35 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.64) at one to five years and 1.19 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.37) beyond five years. When compared to needle suspension procedures, open retropubic colposuspension demonstrated superior outcomes, with lower incontinence rates observed within the first year (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.03), after the first year (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.39 to 0.81), and beyond five years (RR 0.32; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.71). Patient-reported outcomes comparing open and laparoscopic retropubic colposuspension showed no significant differences in incontinence rates at short-, medium-, and long-term follow-up, although the confidence intervals were wide. Two trials comparing the Burch colposuspension technique to the Marshall-Marchetti-Krantz procedure found that incontinence was less common after the Burch procedure at one to five years of follow-up (RR 0.38; 95% CI 0.18 to 0.76). Limited data were available for other follow-up periods. In terms of safety, open retropubic colposuspension did not demonstrate a higher rate of morbidity or complications compared to other open surgical techniques. However, pelvic organ prolapse was more frequently observed following open colposuspension than after anterior colporrhaphy or sling procedures. Conversely, voiding dysfunction was less common after open colposuspension compared to traditional sling surgeries. The authors concluded that open retropubic colposuspension is an effective long-term treatment for stress urinary incontinence, with continence rates of approximately 85% to 90% within the first year and around 70% at five years post-surgery. While newer minimally invasive sling procedures show promise, their long-term efficacy and safety profiles require further investigation. Open colposuspension is associated with a higher risk of pelvic organ prolapse compared to sling operations and anterior colporrhaphy but carries a lower risk of voiding dysfunction than traditional sling surgeries. Laparoscopic colposuspension may offer faster recovery times, but its long-term safety and effectiveness remain uncertain. A brief economic analysis suggested that tension-free vaginal tape (TVT) and laparoscopic colposuspension may be more cost-effective than open retropubic colposuspension.
